unit.title: Prepare for the application of protective coating

summary: This unit teaches you to get welded steelwork ready for paint or hot-dip galvanising. You will read coating specifications and data sheets, dress welds and edges, clean the surface to the standard asked, check humidity, dew point and steel temperature, mask what must stay bare, mix two-pack paints correctly, work out film thicknesses and paint quantities, and record and sign off each stage safely.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It teaches you to get welded steelwork **ready for a protective coating**: paint or hot-dip galvanising. You will read the coating specification and the paint maker's data sheets, dress the welds and edges, clean the surface to the standard asked, check the weather and shop conditions, mask what must not be coated, prepare and mix the coating materials, work out quantities and film thicknesses, and record that each step was done right.

Most early coating failures come from **poor surface preparation**, not from bad paint. A fabricator who leaves spatter, sharp edges, slag or oil on the steel, or lets a painter coat wet steel, has thrown away the client's money. In Jamaica's salty, humid air, a poorly prepared gate or railing can show rust within months.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and fabricators and leading hands who prepare steelwork for painters or galvanisers. At Level 3 you plan the work, lead a small team, make the calculations and sign off each stage.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means on the job
rows: Read the coating specification, the technical data sheets (TDS) and safety data sheets (SDS); plan the order of work, space, access, ventilation and hold points; brief the team.
Control the hazards of grinding, blasting, solvents, two-pack paints and spray equipment; store materials and dispose of waste correctly.
Remove spatter and slag, round sharp edges, repair weld faults, seal crevices, and get frames ready for galvanising.
Degrease, remove salts, clean by hand and power tools or arrange blast cleaning to the standard asked, then check the profile and remove dust.
Measure air temperature, humidity, dew point and steel temperature, and decide whether coating may start.
Mask bolted contact faces, site weld zones, threads, machined faces and anything else the specification names.
Check batches and shelf life; stir, mix and thin as the data sheet says; respect induction time and pot life; set up brushes, rollers and spray equipment.
Work out areas, coverage, litres, tins and wet film targets.
Check the prepared surface and the conditions, sign the hold point before priming, and keep the coating record.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on coatings and corrosion, documents, surface preparation, galvanising, conditions, masking, two-pack paints, film thickness, quantities, safety, storage and records.

A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms) and essays, for example planning the preparation of a staircase, dressing faults, dew point, comparing cleaning methods, mixing a two-pack primer, preparing for galvanising and estimating primer.

**Two group practicals**: dressing, cleaning and masking a welded frame, recording the conditions and brushing a stripe coat; and estimating the paint for a structure, then mixing a two-pack primer and checking the wet film on test panels.

blocks.note: Short answers need exact terms: dew point, sling psychrometer, induction time, DFT, zinc, mill scale, microns, masking, flash point, stripe coat, flash rust, vent holes and hardener. They are all in the key terms at the end.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Rust forms when iron, **oxygen** and **water** meet. Salt (chlorides) and pollution make the water conduct electricity better and speed rusting up many times. Once rust starts at a break in the coating, it creeps under the paint and lifts it.

blocks.note: The whole island is close to the sea. In coastal places such as Port Royal, Negril, Montego Bay, Ocho Rios and Treasure Beach, the sea breeze carries salt spray inland; the humidity is high for most of the year; heavy rain comes in the rainy seasons; and strong sun breaks down some paints. A gate that lasts years in the hills of Manchester can rust through in a few years on the coast. Coastal steel needs a better system, better preparation and thicker films.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Environment
Example
What the coating usually needs
rows: A stair inside an air-conditioned office
A simple system with a modest film thickness
A farm gate in the hills
A good primer and topcoat, edges and welds well covered
A hotel railing a few hundred metres from the sea
Blast cleaning, salt checks, zinc (galvanising or zinc-rich primer) and a thicker multi-coat system
A jetty, or steel in a factory with chemicals
A specialist system chosen by the engineer

blocks.p: Some specifications describe the environment with **corrosivity categories**, from C1 (very low) to C5 (very high) and CX (extreme). The specification then names a system to suit.

head: Way of protecting
How it works
Examples
rows: A thick, tight film keeps water, oxygen and salt away from the steel
Zinc corrodes first and protects the steel, even at small scratches
Pigments in the primer slow rusting at the steel surface

blocks.h: The layers of a paint system

head: Coat
Its job
rows: Grips the steel and protects it from corrosion; the most important coat
An extra brushed coat on edges, corners, welds and bolts, where spray coats are thin
Builds thickness and adds to the barrier
Gives colour and gloss and resists sunlight and weather

head: Type
How it cures
Points to know
rows: Solvent evaporates and the film reacts with oxygen in the air
Easy to use; tolerant of less-than-perfect surfaces
Not to be put straight onto zinc: the film breaks down and peels
A chemical reaction between base and hardener
Chalks in sunlight, so outdoors it needs a topcoat
Has a pot life and minimum and maximum overcoat times
Epoxy or silicate binder full of zinc dust
Topcoat that keeps its colour and gloss in sunlight
Hardeners contain isocyanates, which can cause asthma: respiratory protection is essential
Slow to dry in high humidity
The steel is dipped in molten zinc at about 450 °C
Coats inside and out, bonded to the steel
Needs the frame designed and prepared for it

sections.title: The specification, the data sheets and the plan

head: Document
What it tells you
rows: The coating system; the surface preparation standard (for example Sa 2½ or St 3) and profile; the dry film thickness of each coat; stripe coats; the conditions allowed; masking; inspections, hold points and records.

Volume solids; recommended wet and dry film thickness; theoretical coverage; mixing ratio; induction time; pot life; thinner type and maximum amount; application methods and equipment; drying and overcoat times at different temperatures; conditions limits; shelf life; storage.
Hazards, flash point, PPE, first aid, firefighting, spills, storage, disposal and exposure limits.
Which surfaces are coated; site joints and bolted connections; surfaces to be left bare.

blocks.p: If the specification and a data sheet do not agree, do not choose for yourself: ask the person in charge, and get the answer in writing.

flow: Read the specification, the TDS and the SDS for every product
Walk round the fabrication and mark every fault to dress with chalk
Plan the order: dress, degrease, wash off salts, clean (blast or power tool), remove dust, inspect, mask, stripe coat, prime
Plan the space: supports, lifting, access all round, ventilation, a drying area, and no hot work near the coating area
Book the blast booth and its trained operator if blasting is needed; check the equipment
Estimate and order the paint, thinner, cleaner, masking and PPE; check shelf lives
Brief the team: tasks, hazards, PPE, the standard to reach, and the hold points
Each day: take the condition readings, inspect at each hold point, keep the record

blocks.note: Blasted steel starts to rust again quickly in humid air. Many specifications ask for priming within a few hours of blasting, and always before any rust shows. Plan so that the painter is ready when the blasting is finished.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **hold point** is a stage where work stops until the team leader or inspector has checked and signed it. Typical hold points in coating preparation are: after dressing; after cleaning (standard, profile, dust and salts); and just before priming (conditions, masking and materials).

ul: Give each person a clear task: for example two dressing welds and edges, one degreasing and cleaning, one taking readings, masking and setting up the mixing area.
Show the team the standard to reach, with the reference photographs from the specification.
Go over the hazards and PPE for grinding and for paint, and what to do in a spill or splash.
Check the work at each hold point, coach anyone who is struggling, and stop the work if conditions go out of limits.
At the end of the day, see the area cleaned, waste disposed of, and the record completed.

head: Hazard
Where it comes from
How you control it
rows: Solvent vapour from paint, thinner and cleaner. The vapour is heavier than air and flows along floors to a spark
No welding, grinding or smoking near paint work
Only the day's quantity in the work area
Solvents cause headaches and dizziness, and harm organs over time; epoxy and isocyanate hardeners can cause asthma
The respirator the SDS names, properly fitted
Epoxies and hardeners cause rashes and allergies that can last for life
Chemical-resistant gloves of the type the SDS names
Wash before eating; never clean skin with thinner
Splashes when opening, stirring and mixing
Eyewash ready; rinse a splash with clean water for several minutes and get help
Paint at very high pressure (often well over 100 bar) can be injected through the skin
Tip guard on; trigger lock used
Never point the gun at anyone or wipe the tip under pressure
Relieve the pressure before cleaning or changing the tip
Sparks, flying particles, noise, vibration, dust
Face shield over safety glasses, hearing protection, gloves
Guard on; disc rated for the tool's speed
Abrasive at high speed, rebound, dust, noise, hose whip
Only trained operators, in a proper blast booth
Air-fed blast helmet, protective suit, gloves, boots
Never use sand: its silica dust causes silicosis
Old paint may contain lead or chromates
No dry grinding or burning off
A safe removal method, with protection and controlled waste
Heavy work planned for cooler hours

blocks.note: An airless spray injection can look like a small pinprick, but paint spreads under the skin and can cost a finger or a hand. Go to hospital at once and tell the doctor what was injected.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Keep hot work and coating work apart. A grinder 10 m away can throw sparks into a mixing area full of solvent vapour. Finish or screen off grinding before paint tins are opened.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Store paint and thinner in a cool, dry, ventilated store, out of the sun and away from sparks, with flammable signs and an extinguisher nearby.
Keep lids on and tins upright; use the oldest stock first and check the shelf life.
A store with a zinc roof in the Jamaican sun can get very hot. Check the storage temperature on the TDS, and shade or ventilate the store.
Keep a spill kit, and store tins on a tray that will catch a leak.
Put rags soaked with paint or solvent into a **closed metal bin**, and empty it safely every day. Rags with oil-based paint can heat up and catch fire by themselves.
Waste paint, thinner and empty tins are disposed of as the SDS and local rules say, never down a drain or onto the ground.
Leftover mixed two-pack paint is dealt with as the SDS says, often by letting it cure in the tin in a safe place.
Clean up spills at once with absorbent from the spill kit, and report them.

blocks.p: Paint and zinc follow the shape of the surface. Every fault left in the steel becomes a weak point where rust starts. As the welder, you are in the best position to put these faults right.

head: Fault
Why it matters
What to do
rows: Paint pulls thin over the small balls, and they can be knocked off later, leaving bare steel
Scrape, chip or grind it off; prevent it with correct settings
No coating sticks to it, and zinc will not coat it
Chip and wire-brush every weld completely
Paint flows away from a sharp edge as it dries, so the film there is thin and rust starts
Round them to a small radius (many specifications ask for at least 2 mm) with a grinder or file
A hard, scaly layer on the cut face; paint grips it poorly
Grind the cut face back to clean metal, then round the edges
Paint bridges over them, leaving holes and trapped air where rust starts
Weld-repair or grind smooth, as the specification allows
Trap air; paint is thin on the peaks
Grind to a smooth profile where the specification asks
Layers of steel that lift later and catch the coating
Grind them out; report large ones
Crevices: skip welds on back-to-back angles, lap joints
Water and salt get into gaps that paint cannot reach, and rust swells them open
Seal with a continuous weld or a sealant, as the specification says
Crayon, soapstone, weld fume, anti-spatter spray and oil stop the coating gripping

blocks.p: Some specifications use **preparation grades** (often P1, light, to P3, thorough) to say how far welds, edges and surface faults must be dressed. Check which grade your job asks for.

blocks.note: Dress before you clean. Grinding after blast cleaning spoils the profile and leaves polished patches. Mark faults with chalk on a walk-round, dress them, then check again.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: At the galvaniser the steel is degreased, pickled in acid to remove rust and scale, fluxed, then dipped in **molten zinc at about 450 °C**. Zinc bonds only to clean steel, and anything trapped inside a closed space expands violently in the heat.

head: What to do
Why
rows: Make **vent and drain holes** in every closed hollow section, close to the ends and corners and diagonally opposite, at the size the galvaniser advises
Trapped air or moisture turns to steam in the zinc and can burst the section, which is dangerous. Zinc must flow in and out to coat the inside
Seal-weld lap joints and overlapping plates all round, or leave a gap the galvaniser advises; vent large overlaps
Pickling acid trapped between plates weeps out later as rust stains, and can build pressure in the bath
The acid does not remove slag, so zinc leaves bare spots there
Keep off, or remove, silicone anti-spatter spray, oil-based paint marks, crayon and grease
The galvaniser's cleaning does not lift them, so the zinc will not take. Use a non-silicone anti-spatter and mark parts with metal tags or markers the galvaniser approves
Check the size and weight against the galvaniser's bath, and add lifting points
A part too long for the bath must be double-dipped (agreed beforehand) or made in pieces
Thin or unbalanced frames can warp at 450 °C
Mark threads, holes and moving parts; leave clearance in hinges
Zinc fills threads and closes small gaps; these are cleaned or protected

blocks.note: Talk to the galvaniser **before** the frame is made, not after. Their advice on hole size and position, bath size and lifting saves cutting and re-welding later.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Remove oil, grease, cutting fluid and marker with a solvent wipe or a detergent wash and fresh-water rinse
Wash off salt and dirt with clean fresh water (high-pressure where needed); let the steel dry
Remove rust and mill scale by hand and power tools, or by abrasive blast cleaning, to the standard the specification gives
Remove dust and spent abrasive
Inspect: the cleanliness standard, the profile, salts and dust
Prime before any rust returns

blocks.p: Oil comes off **first** because grinding and blasting spread it over the steel and drive it into the surface, and oily abrasive spreads it further. A simple check is the **water-break test**: wet the surface with clean water. If the water stays as an unbroken film, the surface is free of oil; if it breaks into beads and islands, oil is still there.

Wire brushes, scrapers, chipping hammers, needle guns, power wire cup brushes, flap discs and abrasive discs remove **loose** rust, loose mill scale and flaking paint. They leave tight mill scale and give little **profile** (roughness), and a power wire brush used too long polishes the steel so the paint grips poorly. Standards St 2 (thorough) and St 3 (very thorough) describe the result. This method suits small areas, repairs, site touch-ups and coatings that the TDS says will tolerate it.

Abrasive (such as steel grit, steel shot or a mineral grit) is thrown at the steel by compressed air or a spinning wheel. It removes all mill scale and rust and leaves a rough **profile** that high-performance primers need. **Mill scale** is the hard, blue-grey oxide skin left on hot-rolled steel by the mill; it cracks and lifts off later, taking the paint with it, so high-performance systems need it removed.

head: Grade (ISO 8501-1)
Near US equivalent
What the surface looks like
rows: Loose mill scale, rust and paint removed
Most mill scale, rust and paint removed; what is left is firmly stuck
Only slight stains or shadows remain; the usual standard for high-performance systems
Even metallic colour all over, with no stains

blocks.p: The standards come with **reference photographs**. Compare the cleaned steel with the photograph for its starting condition (rust grade A to D) and the grade asked for.

blocks.note: At the Centre, abrasive blasting is done only by trained people, in a proper blast booth, with an air-fed helmet and protective suit. Never blast in the open shop.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: The **surface profile** (anchor pattern) is the pattern of tiny peaks and valleys left by blasting, measured from peak to valley in **microns** (µm). The specification or TDS gives a range, commonly about 50–75 µm for many high-performance primers. Too little profile and the primer grips poorly; too much and peaks poke through the primer and rust spots appear.

ul: **Replica tape**: pressed onto the surface and rubbed so it takes the shape of the profile, then read with a spring micrometer.
**Profile comparator**: a reference disc the surface is compared with by eye and touch.
**Needle depth gauge**: a gauge whose needle drops into the valleys.
Grit gives a sharp, angular profile; shot gives a rounded one. Larger abrasive and higher pressure give a deeper profile.

blocks.p: After blasting, remove dust and abrasive with a vacuum, a brush, or clean, dry, oil-free compressed air. Check with the **tape test**: press clear adhesive tape onto the surface, pull it off and compare the dust on it with the rating the specification allows.

Salt settles on steel stored near the sea or outdoors, and blasting does not remove it all: it can drive salt into the profile. Under paint, salt draws water through the film and causes **blisters** and rust. A **patch test** (a small adhesive cell filled with pure water, which is then drawn off and measured) checks the salt level against the specification's limit. If it is too high: wash with fresh water, dry, re-blast if needed, and test again.

**Flash rust** is a light, even orange rust that forms quickly on freshly blasted or freshly washed steel. If it appears before priming, the steel is cleaned again to the specified standard. Do not prime over it unless the specification and the primer's TDS allow a stated light grade.

blocks.note: In humid coastal shops, flash rust can appear within a few hours, especially overnight. Blast only what can be primed the same day, keep blasted steel under cover and off the ground, and check the dew point before you start.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Reading
What it means
rows: The temperature of the air, read on the dry-bulb thermometer
The water vapour in the air as a percentage of the most it could hold at that temperature. Warm air can hold more
The temperature at which that water vapour starts to condense as water on a cool surface
The temperature of the steel surface itself, which can be well above or below the air temperature

blocks.p: If the steel is at or close to the dew point, a film of water forms on it, often too thin to see. Paint put over it grips poorly and rust starts underneath. The usual rule in specifications and data sheets is: **the steel must be at least 3 °C above the dew point**, the RH below the TDS maximum (often 85%), and the air and steel temperatures inside the TDS limits. The rule must hold while the coating is applied and while it dries.

head: Instrument
Use
rows: A dry-bulb and a wet-bulb thermometer, whirled in the air until the wet-bulb reading stops falling. The two readings, with tables or a calculator, give the RH and dew point. Keep the wick clean and wet with distilled water
Reads air temperature and RH, and usually works out the dew point; it must be in calibration
A magnetic dial thermometer or a digital probe placed on the steel itself. Read the coldest parts: shaded faces and the undersides
Turn the readings into a dew point

head: Air
RH
Dew point
Steel
Steel above dew point
Decision
rows: May start, if the other TDS limits are met
Stop: too close to the dew point, and RH too high

blocks.note: Record the readings at the start of work, at the times the specification sets (often every few hours) and whenever the weather changes, with the time and your name.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: **Early morning:** steel left outside cools under the open night sky and can be colder than the air and below the dew point, so it is wet with dew even when the air feels dry. Wait until the sun or the shop has warmed the steel and the dew has gone, then take readings.
**Afternoon showers** raise the humidity quickly and cool the steel. Watch the sky and take readings again.

**Steel in full sun** can reach 50–60 °C or more, above the TDS maximum for many paints. Solvent then flashes off too fast, giving dry spray, pinholes, poor flow and poor grip. Coat in the shade, or in the morning or late afternoon.
**Sea breeze** carries salt, blows overspray and dust about, and dries paint unevenly. Coat under cover where you can.
**Indoors**, ventilate for the solvent, but keep blasting and grinding dust away from wet paint.

head: What is masked
Why
How
rows: Contact (faying) faces of friction-grip bolted joints
Ordinary paint lowers the friction, so the joint may slip
Mask them, or coat them only with the slip-rated coating the specification names
A strip each side of a joint to be welded on site
Coating burns in the weld heat, giving fumes and porosity, and is damaged anyway
Mask a strip (often about 50–100 mm each side, as the specification says), or use only a weldable primer
Threads, machined faces, bearing surfaces, bolt holes
Surfaces to be cast into concrete
The specification may ask for bare steel there

blocks.p: **Masking** means covering an area with tape, plugs, caps or a guard so no coating reaches it. Use tape that suits the coating and the temperature: in Jamaican heat some tape adhesives soften and leave residue. Remove tape at the time the specification or tape maker gives, usually once the coating is touch dry, for a clean edge.

flow: Check each product's name and colour against the specification; record the batch numbers; check the shelf-life date
Look at the paint: no skin, gel or hard-packed settlement that will not stir in
Stir the base well, with a power mixer at low speed if needed, until all the settled solids are mixed back in
Two-pack: measure base and hardener at the exact ratio on the TDS (by volume or weight), add the hardener to the base and mix thoroughly, scraping the sides and bottom
Leave it to stand for the induction time if the TDS gives one
Add thinner only of the type, and up to the amount, the TDS allows
Write down the mixing time: the pot life starts now. Mix only what can be used within it

head: Term
What it means
rows: The two parts of a two-pack paint. The **hardener** (curing agent) reacts with the base to cure the film
The proportions to mix, for example 4:1 by volume: 4 parts base to 1 part hardener
A standing time some paints need after mixing and before use, so the reaction can start
How long the mixed paint stays usable. It is shorter in heat: it often roughly halves for every 10 °C rise, so check the TDS figure for your temperature
The minimum and maximum time before the next coat
How long the unopened tins stay usable in storage

ul: Too little hardener: the film may never cure properly, stays soft and fails.
Too much hardener: the film can be brittle and weak.
Never use part-tins without measuring them, and never mix products or batches the TDS does not allow.
Never thin paint that has started to gel to make it last longer: it will not cure properly.

blocks.p: Use only the thinner the TDS names, and no more than its maximum. Too much thinner gives a thin film, runs and low dry film thickness; the wrong thinner can make the paint curdle or cure badly. Remember that thinner also changes the wet film you must apply (see the next section).

A **stripe coat** is an extra coat **brushed** onto edges, corners, welds, bolts and small gaps, where spray coats are thin. The brush works the paint into weld ripples and pits and builds film on edges. A slightly different colour from the full coat shows where it has gone. The specification says when stripe coats go on (often before each full coat).

head: Method
Suits
Checks before use
rows: Stripe coats, small areas, edges, welds
Right type and size; clean; no loose bristles
Right nap for the paint; not for edges or welds
Clean, dry, oil-free air (water and oil traps working); pressures
Large areas and thick coatings, quickly
Hose rated for the pressure and undamaged; fittings tight
Tip guard on and trigger lock working
Tip size as the TDS says; test on scrap

blocks.p: If the next coat goes on **before** the minimum time, solvent is trapped and the film may wrinkle or stay soft. If it goes on **after** the maximum, the coat below may be too hard for the next one to grip. Follow the TDS: usually the surface is cleaned and roughened (lightly abraded or sweep-blasted) first, or a tie coat is used. Overcoat times are shorter in heat, and an epoxy primer left in the sun also chalks and must be washed and roughened before overcoating.
Film thickness is measured in **microns** (µm): one micron is a thousandth of a millimetre, so 100 µm = 0.1 mm.

blocks.h: Wet film, dry film and volume solids

blocks.p: **Volume solids (VS)** is the percentage of the wet paint's volume that stays as dry film; the rest is solvent that evaporates. **WFT** is the wet film thickness, measured as you apply. **DFT** is the **dry film thickness**, what the specification asks for.

ul: **DFT = WFT × VS ÷ 100**
**WFT = DFT × 100 ÷ VS** (no thinner)
**WFT = DFT × (100 + % thinner) ÷ VS** (with thinner)
Use it **straight after** applying, on the wet film, before the solvent goes.
Press it square onto the surface and lift it off. The thickness lies between the last tooth that is wetted with paint and the first one that is not.
Take readings across the whole area, wipe the comb clean after each one, and adjust your application (more passes, slower movement) to reach the target.
The DFT is checked after drying, by the inspector, with a calibrated magnetic or electronic gauge.
Too thick is a fault as well: it wastes paint, traps solvent, cures slowly and can crack.

blocks.h: Coverage and how much to order

blocks.p: **Theoretical coverage (m² per litre) = VS% × 10 ÷ DFT in µm.** It assumes no losses at all.

flow: Work out the area from the drawings: for sections, the surface area per metre (from steel tables, or the perimeter) × the length; for plates, both faces
Work out the theoretical coverage from the volume solids and the DFT
Divide the area by the coverage: the theoretical litres
Add the loss allowance the job sets: paint lost in overspray, on brushes and rollers, in the pot and on rough surfaces
Round up to whole tins (or whole kits for two-pack), and repeat for each coat
Check the paint can all be used within its shelf life, and mix only what fits the pot life

blocks.p: Loss allowances vary with the method and the job: often about 10–20% for brush and roller on simple shapes, and 30–50% or more for spraying open frames outdoors in wind. Use the figure the job or your instructor gives.

head: Step
Worked example
rows: A frame of 50 × 50 mm square hollow section, sealed at the ends: perimeter 200 mm, so 0.2 m² per metre. 280 m of it = 56 m²
4 L tins: 14.56 ÷ 4 = 3.64, so order 4 tins (16 L)

head: Check
How
rows: Walk round with the specification: no spatter, slag, sharp edges or open weld faults
Water-break test; look; wipe with a clean white rag
Compare with the reference photographs (for example St 3 or Sa 2½)
Replica tape, comparator or depth gauge, against the specified range
Air temperature, RH, dew point and steel temperature: steel at least 3 °C above the dew point and inside the TDS limits
In place on every named area
Right products, batches in date, mixing and pot life noted, equipment checked, wet film combs ready

blocks.p: The **coating record** shows the job and item, the date and times, every reading, the standard and profile reached, the products and batch numbers, the mixing time, any thinner added, the wet film readings, who did each step and the sign-off at each hold point. It proves the work met the specification, and if the coating fails later it shows where to look.
Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and work on it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain why steel rusts, why salt air makes it worse, and how barrier, sacrificial and inhibitive coatings protect it.
I can name the coats in a paint system and say what each one does.
I can find what I need in a coating specification, a technical data sheet and a safety data sheet.
I can plan the preparation of a fabrication, with the order of work, space, ventilation and hold points, and brief a team.
I can control the hazards of grinding, blasting, solvents, two-pack paints and airless spray, and give first aid for an eye splash.
I can store paint safely and dispose of rags and waste correctly.
I can name the faults to dress before coating and say why each one matters.
I can prepare a frame for hot-dip galvanising, including vent and drain holes.
I can put the cleaning steps in the right order and explain why oil comes off first.
I can compare hand and power tool cleaning with blast cleaning, and describe the Sa and St grades.
I can explain surface profile and how it is measured, and deal with dust, salts and flash rust.
I can measure and record air temperature, humidity, dew point and steel temperature, and decide whether coating may start.
I can mask the areas a specification names and say why.
I can mix a two-pack paint at the right ratio, and explain induction time, pot life and overcoat times.
I can work out wet film targets, coverage, litres and tins, including thinner and losses.
I can use a wet film comb and adjust my application to hit the target.
I can inspect a prepared surface, sign the hold point and complete the coating record.

terms: Abrasive blast cleaning
Cleaning steel by throwing abrasive at it at high speed; removes mill scale and rust and leaves a profile
Coverage (spreading rate)
The area one litre of paint covers at a given dry film thickness, in m² per litre
Dew point
The temperature at which moisture in the air starts to condense on a cool surface
Dry film thickness (DFT)
The thickness of a coat once it has dried, in microns
Faying surface
A contact face of a bolted joint
Flash point
The lowest temperature at which a liquid gives off enough vapour to catch fire
Flash rust
Light rust that forms quickly on freshly blasted or washed steel
Hardener
The curing part mixed into the base of a two-pack paint; also called the curing agent
Hold point
A stage where work stops until it has been checked and signed
Hot-dip galvanising
Coating steel by dipping it in molten zinc
Induction time
The time some mixed two-pack paints must stand before use
Masking
Covering an area with tape, plugs or a guard so that no coating reaches it
Micron (µm)
One thousandth of a millimetre; the unit for film thickness
Mill scale
The hard, blue-grey oxide layer left on hot-rolled steel by the steel mill
Overcoat interval
The minimum and maximum time before the next coat may go on
Pot life
How long a mixed two-pack paint stays usable
Primer
The first coat: it grips the steel and helps stop corrosion
Relative humidity (RH)
The moisture in the air as a percentage of the most it can hold at that temperature
Safety data sheet (SDS)
The maker's document on hazards, PPE, first aid, storage and disposal
Sling psychrometer
An instrument with wet-bulb and dry-bulb thermometers, whirled to find the humidity
Soluble salts
Salt on the steel surface that draws water under paint and causes blisters
Stripe coat
An extra coat brushed onto welds, edges and corners to build up film there
Surface profile
The peaks and valleys left by blast cleaning that help the paint grip; also called the anchor pattern
Technical data sheet (TDS)
The paint maker's document on how to prepare, mix, apply and dry the product
Vent and drain holes
Holes in hollow sections that let air escape and zinc flow in and out during galvanising
Volume solids (VS)
The percentage of the wet paint's volume that stays as dry film
Wet film thickness (WFT)
The thickness of a coat as it is applied, measured with a comb
Zinc-rich primer
A primer full of zinc dust that protects steel sacrificially

c1.title: Fishermen's shelter frames at Treasure Beach
c1.text: Owen, a Level 3 trainee, leads the preparation of welded steel frames for a fishermen's shelter at Treasure Beach, St Elizabeth, about 50 m from the sea. The frames have stood outside on the beach for two weeks. They have flame-cut edges, spatter, and back-to-back angles joined with short skip welds. The specification asks for welds and edges to be dressed, degreasing, a salt test, blast cleaning to Sa 2½ with a 50–75 µm profile, then a zinc-rich epoxy primer, an epoxy intermediate coat and a polyurethane topcoat.

c2.title: Handrail panels for galvanising in Bull Bay
c2.text: Natalie's shop in Bull Bay, St Andrew, is making 40 handrail panels for hot-dip galvanising. Each panel is a frame of 50 mm square hollow section with 25 mm square hollow balusters fully welded all round inside it. To keep spatter down, a welder has been using a silicone-based anti-spatter spray, and the job numbers have been painted on each panel in oil-based paint. The panels are drawn 3.2 m long; the galvaniser's bath is 3 m long.

c3.title: Morning readings in Port Antonio
c3.text: In an open-sided shop in Port Antonio, Portland, Kerron is to stripe-coat and then apply the intermediate coat to beams that were primed yesterday and left outside overnight. The data sheet says: steel at least 3 °C above the dew point, relative humidity no more than 85%, steel no hotter than 50 °C. At 6:30 a.m. he reads: air 24 °C, RH 90%, dew point 22 °C, steel 21 °C. At 10:30 a.m.: air 30 °C, RH 70%, dew point 24 °C, steel 31 °C. By 1:30 p.m. the beams in full sun read 55 °C.

c4.title: Mixing an epoxy primer in Christiana
c4.text: In a shop in Christiana, Manchester, Shanique is preparing a two-pack epoxy primer. The data sheet gives: mixing ratio 4:1 by volume (base to hardener); induction time 10 minutes; pot life 4 hours at 20 °C, shorter when hotter; thinning up to 5% with the named thinner; volume solids 60%; DFT 100 µm; overcoat interval 6 hours minimum and 7 days maximum. The shop is at 32 °C, and she needs about 2.5 litres of mixed paint for the morning.

c5.title: Estimating primer for a footbridge in Lucea
c5.text: Jodian is estimating the primer for a steel footbridge in Lucea, Hanover. The drawings give 84 m² of steel to coat. The primer has 50% volume solids and must be applied at 80 µm DFT. Because it will be sprayed outdoors in the sea breeze, the job allows 40% for losses. The primer comes in 4-litre tins.

questions.q: What should be done about the back-to-back angles joined with skip welds?
o: Fill the gaps with primer as the frames are being coated
Seal the gaps with a full weld or the named sealant
Leave them, as the gaps let rainwater drain out freely
Blast the gaps harder so the abrasive cleans right inside
questions.why: Salt water gets into the gaps between the skip welds where paint cannot reach, and the rust swells the angles apart. Sealing the crevice is part of dressing the fabrication.

questions.q: The salt test on the frames is above the specification's limit. What should Owen do?
o: Prime at once, so the primer seals the salt in under the coating
Wipe the steel down with thinner, then go straight on to priming
Blast the frames, since blasting removes all of the salt anyway
Wash with fresh water, let it dry, and test again before priming
questions.why: Salt left under paint draws water through the film and causes blisters, and blasting alone does not remove it all. Washing with fresh water, drying and re-testing brings it within the limit.

questions.q: Which order of work is right for these frames?
o: Blast, dress welds and edges, degrease, test for salt, then prime
Degrease, blast, dress welds and edges, remove dust, then prime
Dress welds and edges, degrease, wash off salt, blast, then prime
Wash off salt, blast, degrease, dress welds and edges, then prime
questions.why: Dressing comes first so grinding does not spoil the blast profile; oil comes off before blasting so it is not spread; salts are washed off before blasting; then dust is removed and the steel primed.

questions.q: After blasting, replica tape on the frames reads 30 µm. What should happen?
o: Prime it, since a smoother surface takes the paint more evenly
Re-blast to reach 50–75 µm, for example with coarser abrasive
Apply a thicker coat of primer to make up for the low reading
Rough it up with a power wire brush and then go on to priming
questions.why: 30 µm is below the specified 50–75 µm profile, so the zinc-rich primer will not grip as it should. The steel is re-blasted, often with a coarser abrasive, until the profile is in range.

questions.q: Where should the vent and drain holes go in each sealed baluster?
o: Near both ends, on opposite sides, as the galvaniser advises
In the middle of each baluster, on the side that will not be seen
Only at the bottom end, so that the zinc can drain out of it
None are needed if the balusters are welded all round and sealed
questions.why: A fully sealed hollow can burst in molten zinc, and zinc must flow through to coat the inside. Holes near both ends, placed as the galvaniser advises, let air out and zinc in and out.

questions.q: Some panels have already been sprayed with the silicone anti-spatter. What should be done?
o: Nothing, as the galvaniser's acid will dissolve it along with the rust
Wash it off with water, since silicone sprays are water-based products
Ask the galvaniser to dip those panels for longer to burn the film off
Remove it as the galvaniser advises before the panels are dipped
questions.why: The galvaniser's degreasing and pickling do not lift silicone, so the zinc will not take and bare spots are left. It must be removed first, usually by blasting or grinding; from now on a non-silicone spray is used.

questions.q: What should Natalie do about the panel length and the 3 m bath?
o: Make the panels as drawn and let the galvaniser solve it on the day
Cut each panel in two after it has been galvanised to make it fit
Agree double-dipping or a redesign with the galvaniser first
Galvanise 3 m of each panel and paint the last 200 mm by hand
questions.why: A part longer than the bath must be double-dipped, which the galvaniser must agree to, or the design changed. That is settled before fabrication, not when the panels arrive.

questions.q: Why is the oil-based paint used for the job numbers a problem?
o: Pickling will not lift it, so the zinc leaves bare spots there
Oil-based paint turns into a toxic gas when it is dipped in the zinc
The job numbers will show through the zinc on the finished handrail
Molten zinc reacts with oil paint and makes the coating far too thick
questions.why: Paint marks are not lifted by pickling, so the zinc does not bond there and bare patches result. Mark galvanised work with metal tags or markers the galvaniser approves.

questions.q: What should Kerron decide at 6:30 a.m.?
o: Start: the air is 2 °C above the dew point, which is close enough
Start, but thin the paint more so that it dries before the dew forms
Wait: the steel is below the dew point and the humidity is too high
Start on the stripe coat by brush, as only spraying needs dry steel
questions.why: The rule is about the steel, not the air: at 21 °C the steel is below the 22 °C dew point, so it is almost certainly wet, and the RH of 90% is above the 85% limit. Coating waits.

questions.q: What do the 10:30 a.m. readings tell Kerron?
o: 7 °C above the dew point, RH within limits: he may start
The steel is only 1 °C above the air, so he must still wait
The RH of 70% is still too high for any coating work to start
The steel is 6 °C above the dew point, which is too close to it
questions.why: 31 °C steel minus a 24 °C dew point is 7 °C, more than the 3 °C needed, and 70% RH is under the 85% maximum. He records the readings and keeps checking through the day.

questions.q: At 1:30 p.m. the beams in the sun are at 55 °C. What should Kerron do?
o: Carry on, as hot steel helps the paint dry faster and harder
Add extra thinner so the paint flows before the solvent flashes
Spray the beams with water to cool them, then carry on painting
Stop coating those beams until they are shaded and below 50 °C
questions.why: Above the data sheet's 50 °C limit the solvent flashes off too fast, giving dry spray, pinholes and poor grip. Work in the shade, or at a cooler time; wetting the steel just adds water.

questions.q: Which instrument gives Kerron the steel temperature?
o: The dry-bulb thermometer on the sling psychrometer
A surface thermometer placed on the steel itself
The wet-bulb thermometer on the sling psychrometer
A digital hygrometer hung on a nail in the shop
questions.why: Psychrometers and hygrometers read the air, which can be far hotter or cooler than the steel. A magnetic or probe surface thermometer on the steel, on the coolest faces, gives the reading the rule needs.

questions.q: How much base and hardener should Shanique measure for 2.5 litres of mixed paint?
o: 2.0 L of base and 0.5 L of hardener
2.5 L of base and 0.5 L of hardener
1.875 L of base and 0.625 L of hardener
2.25 L of base and 0.25 L of hardener
questions.why: A 4:1 ratio makes 5 parts, so each part is 2.5 ÷ 5 = 0.5 L: 4 × 0.5 = 2.0 L of base and 0.5 L of hardener. The other choices give ratios of 5:1, 3:1 and 9:1.

questions.q: Why should Shanique mix only a small batch at a time today?
o: At 32 °C the pot life is much shorter, so it may gel
Small batches need less hardener, so the cost of the job is lower
The induction time is longer in the heat, so big batches wait
Two-pack paint can only be mixed accurately in small amounts
questions.why: Pot life shortens as the temperature rises, often roughly halving for every 10 °C. At 32 °C the paint may have far less than 4 hours, so she notes the mixing time and mixes only what can be used.

questions.q: If Shanique adds the full 5% of thinner, which wet film should she aim for?
o: 167 µm
160 µm
105 µm
175 µm
questions.why: WFT = DFT × (100 + % thinner) ÷ VS = 100 × 105 ÷ 60 = 175 µm. Without thinner it would be 167 µm; thinner adds liquid that will evaporate, so more wet film is needed for the same dry film.

questions.q: The primer went on nine days ago and the next coat is due today. What should be done first?
o: Apply the next coat straight away, as the primer is fully hard
Clean and roughen it, or treat it as the data sheet says
Apply a second full coat of primer, then the next coat a week later
Thin the next coat well so that it can soak into the primer
questions.why: Nine days is past the 7-day maximum, so the hard primer may not let the next coat grip. The data sheet gives the remedy, usually cleaning and lightly abrading or sweep-blasting the surface first.

questions.q: What is the primer's theoretical coverage?
o: 4.0 m² per litre
6.25 m² per litre
16 m² per litre
62.5 m² per litre
questions.why: Coverage = VS% × 10 ÷ DFT = 50 × 10 ÷ 80 = 6.25 m² per litre, before any losses.

questions.q: How many 4-litre tins should Jodian order?
o: 4 tins
6 tins
3 tins
5 tins
questions.why: Theory: 84 ÷ 6.25 = 13.44 L. With 40% losses: 13.44 × 1.4 = 18.8 L. 18.8 ÷ 4 = 4.7, rounded up to 5 tins. Four tins would cover the theory but not the losses.

questions.q: The tip of an airless spray gun blocks part-way through a coat. What should the painter do first?
o: Hold a finger over the tip so the pressure blows the blockage back
Turn the pump pressure up to force the blockage out of the tip
Lock the trigger and release the pressure before touching it
Wipe the tip with a rag while pointing the gun into the pail
questions.why: Paint at airless pressure can be injected through the skin, so nothing touches the tip while it is under pressure. Lock the trigger and relieve the pressure first, then clear or reverse the tip as the maker says.

questions.q: A specification asks for blast cleaning to Sa 2½. What should the cleaned steel look like?
o: Bright metal of even colour, with no stains at all
Loose rust and scale gone; firm mill scale may stay
Only slight stains or shadows left on the steel
Most of the scale gone; firmly stuck residues left
questions.why: Sa 2½ (very thorough, near-white) leaves only slight stains or shadows. No stains at all is Sa 3; loose material only is Sa 1; and firmly stuck residues left is Sa 2.
